title: OPQ and learned rotations
summary: An orthogonal rotation leaves all distances unchanged but changes which dimensions land in which PQ subspace, which is free to exploit. Measured, the textbook variance-imbalance motivation did not apply to this model, but rotating into a decorrelated basis still bought 5 points of recall, while the expensive iterative refinement kept improving reconstruction error without improving recall.
html:
Since Day 21 I have been cutting 384 dimensions into contiguous blocks of 16 and treating each block as an independent subspace. Dimensions 0 to 15 go together because they are next to each other, which is not a reason.

Today is about fixing that with a rotation, why that is allowed, and a measurement that did not go the way the textbook says it should.

Why you are allowed to rotate

An orthogonal matrix R satisfies R^T R = I, which means it preserves inner products:

(Rx) . (Ry)  =  x^T R^T R y  =  x^T y  =  x . y

Rotate every vector and every query by the same R and all your distances are unchanged. The geometry is identical, the nearest neighbours are identical, and recall against exact search is unaffected. It is a free change of basis.

Free for the geometry, but not for PQ, because PQ does not see the geometry. It sees axis-aligned blocks of coordinates, and a rotation changes which coordinates end up in which block. So you can shuffle the information between subspaces however you like, at zero cost to correctness, and that is the whole opportunity.

The two things a rotation can fix

Variance imbalance. Every subspace gets the same 256 centroids. If one block carries ten times the variance of another, the busy block is under-resourced and the quiet one is wasting capacity.

Correlation across blocks. PQ's whole premise is that subspaces are independent, which is what lets the codebooks multiply. If a dimension in block 3 is strongly correlated with one in block 17, you are spending bits in two places to encode one fact.

The first measurement, which went wrong

I checked the variance imbalance on my embeddings, expecting to find the motivating problem:

variance per subspace, 24 contiguous blocks of 16 dims
min 0.0369   max 0.0428   ratio 1.16x   std/mean 0.033

Essentially balanced. The textbook motivation does not apply here at all.

The reason is that this model's output dimensions carry no ordering. They are not sorted by importance the way PCA components are, so any contiguous slice gets an average mix by accident. If you fed PQ data that was PCA-ordered, block 0 would hold most of the variance and block 23 would hold almost none, and the imbalance story would be real. With a raw learned embedding it is not.

So I expected rotations to do nothing. Here is what actually happened, same 24 bytes per vector throughout:

1. plain PQ, contiguous split        recon MSE 0.43364   recall@10 0.628
2. + random orthogonal rotation      recon MSE 0.43776   recall@10 0.610
3. + PCA, variance dealt evenly      recon MSE 0.27886   recall@10 0.680
4. OPQ, 6 alternating iterations      recon MSE 0.31682   recall@10 0.662

Row 2 confirms the first finding: a random rotation buys nothing, because there was no imbalance to fix and randomising a balanced split just gives you a different balanced split.

Row 3 is the result. Rotate into the PCA basis, then deal the components across subspaces round robin, highest variance first, so each block gets one of the top 24 components, one of the next 24, and so on. Reconstruction error drops 36 percent and recall gains 5.2 points for free.

Since the variance was already balanced, that gain cannot be variance balancing. It is the second effect: PCA components are uncorrelated by construction, so dealing them into blocks gives PQ subspaces that are genuinely closer to independent, which is the assumption its codebooks rest on.

The expensive version, and a warning

That was parametric OPQ: one eigendecomposition, deterministic, seconds. The non-parametric version alternates instead, refitting codebooks and then solving for the best rotation given them, which is an orthogonal Procrustes problem you get from an SVD. Starting from the PCA solution, which is the standard initialisation:

parametric OPQ (PCA init, 0 iters)   MSE 0.27886   recall 0.680
non-parametric OPQ,  1 iteration     MSE 0.27648   recall 0.662
non-parametric OPQ,  2 iterations    MSE 0.27480   recall 0.678
non-parametric OPQ,  4 iterations    MSE 0.27323   recall 0.687
non-parametric OPQ,  8 iterations    MSE 0.27179   recall 0.678

Look at the two columns separately. MSE falls monotonically, exactly as the optimisation promises. Recall does not follow it. Eight iterations buy a 2.5 percent reduction in reconstruction error and leave recall wobbling inside its own noise.

That is a worked example of a proxy objective coming apart from the real one. OPQ minimises reconstruction error because that is what is tractable, and reconstruction error is a decent stand-in for ranking quality right up until it stops being one. Past a point you are optimising a number that has quietly stopped correlating with the thing you ship.

Be careful with my numbers in both directions. At 300 queries one changed slot is 0.033 points, so the 0.628 to 0.680 jump is a real effect and the 0.662 to 0.687 wobble mostly is not. My corpus is also small enough that the codebooks are undertrained (Day 21). What I would stand behind: parametric OPQ was worth 5 points and cost nothing, and the iterative refinement was not visibly worth its runtime here.

What to actually do

Apply the rotation once at build time, store the matrix, apply it to every query. It is a d x d matrix, 590 KB at 384 dimensions, and one matrix multiply per query against a cache-resident matrix. Against the gains it is free, and every serious library offers it as a flag. Turn it on.

If your data is already PCA-reduced or otherwise ordered by importance, the variance argument applies to you too and the gain will be larger than mine. If you are feeding raw embedding output, expect the decorrelation effect I measured rather than the textbook one.

Phase 2 so far assumes the index lives in memory. Tomorrow it does not: DiskANN, and what changes when the vectors are on SSD and only the compressed codes are resident.
exercise:
1. Check your own variance balance. Centre your vectors, split them into m contiguous blocks, and print the total variance of each block. If max over min is near 1, the textbook motivation for OPQ does not apply to your model either, and you should expect the decorrelation effect rather than the balancing one.

2. Implement parametric OPQ. Eigendecompose the covariance, sort components by eigenvalue, then deal them round robin into m groups so each subspace gets a spread of variances. Rotate, fit PQ, measure reconstruction error against the unrotated baseline. Ten lines, and in my run it was the entire benefit.

3. Watch a proxy drift. Run a few alternating OPQ iterations and record reconstruction MSE and recall after each. Plot both. The point at which they stop moving together is the point at which further optimisation is spending your time on the wrong number, and seeing it once makes you suspicious of proxy metrics permanently.
